lessons.title: Process Concepts, States, PCBs, Threads, and Scheduling Queues

learningObjectives.text: Explain process memory layout, execution state, and lifecycle transitions.

materialSections.title: Process concept and memory layout
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: A process is an active program in execution, with a program counter, processor registers, and resources; a passive executable becomes a process when loaded into memory.
explanation: A process progresses sequentially and is represented by its current program counter and register contents. Its memory normally contains text, data, heap, and stack sections.

Text and data sizes are fixed during a run, while heap and stack can grow and shrink toward one another without overlapping. A C program further separates initialized and uninitialized data and stores argc and argv separately.

keyTerms.definition: A program in execution with active state and resources.

workedExamples.title: Function-call stack
workedExamples.body: A function call pushes an activation record, and returning pops it.

examTips.body: Distinguish fixed text/data from dynamically changing heap/stack.

recap: A process is active; a program file is passive.
Text and data are fixed during execution.

materialSections.title: Process states, traces, and queueing models
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: The five-state model distinguishes new, ready, running, waiting, and terminated processes and connects those states through dispatch, timeout, event wait, and event occurrence.
explanation: A ready process waits for a processor, while a waiting process awaits an event such as I/O completion. At one instant only one process can run on a processor core, although many can be ready or waiting.
The execution trace uses a dispatcher at address 100 to switch among three loaded processes. Queueing diagrams show either one blocked queue or separate queues for distinct events.

keyTerms.definition: Waiting to be assigned to a processor.

workedExamples.title: Trace diagnosis

materialSections.title: PCB, Linux representation, and multithreading
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: The PCB stores all information needed to start or restart a process, including execution, scheduling, memory, accounting, and I/O state; Linux represents this information with task_struct.
explanation: On an interrupt, process state is saved in the PCB so execution can resume correctly. Linux links active task_struct records in a doubly linked list and keeps current pointing to the executing process.

A thread owns a thread ID, program counter, register set, and stack while sharing its process code, data, open files, and signals. Multithreading supports responsiveness, resource sharing, economy, and scalability.

materialSections.title: Scheduling goals, process classes, queues, and swapping
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Multiprogramming keeps a process running to maximize CPU use, while time sharing switches cores frequently enough to support interaction.
explanation: The scheduler selects a ready process for a CPU core. The degree of multiprogramming counts processes in memory; I/O-bound processes spend more time on I/O, while CPU-bound processes compute for longer stretches.

Processes move among ready and wait queues after dispatch, I/O, child waits, interrupts, and time-slice expiry. Swapping can temporarily move a process to disk when memory is overcommitted and later restore it.

lessons.title: Context Switching, Process Operations, and Shared-Memory IPC

learningObjectives.text: Explain context switches and the isolation benefits of multiprocess browser architecture.

materialSections.title: Context switching and browser process isolation
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: A context switch saves the old process state and restores the new process state through their PCBs; the switching interval is overhead rather than useful work.
explanation: Context-switch duration depends on hardware support and PCB or OS complexity. Interrupt handling requires saving enough context to suspend and later resume the running process.
Chrome separates one browser process, per-site renderer processes, and per-plugin processes. Renderer isolation and sandbox restrictions limit the impact of a site crash or exploit.
materialSections.body:
Context-switch duration depends on hardware support and PCB or OS complexity. Interrupt handling requires saving enough context to suspend and later resume the running process.

Chrome separates one browser process, per-site renderer processes, and per-plugin processes. Renderer isolation and sandbox restrictions limit the impact of a site crash or exploit.

keyTerms.definition: Saving one process context and restoring another.
A Chrome process that renders a web page and handles its content.

workedExamples.title: Crash isolation
workedExamples.body: A website crash affects its renderer while other browser processes remain unharmed.

commonMistakes.misconception: Context-switch time performs user work.
commonMistakes.correction: It is pure overhead during which the system performs no useful work.

examTips.body: Remember that complexity and hardware support affect switching time.

materialSections.title: Process creation, resources, and UNIX calls
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Processes are created dynamically in parent-child trees and identified by unique integer process identifiers.
explanation: A child may obtain resources from the OS or a parent subset; parent and child may share all, some, or no resources. Execution can be concurrent or the parent can wait, and the child can duplicate the address space or load another program.

In UNIX, fork() creates the process, exec() replaces its memory with a new program, and wait() blocks a parent for child termination. Successful fork returns the child PID to the parent and zero to the child; systemd with PID 1 roots user processes.

materialSections.title: Termination and IPC foundations
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: A process normally exits through exit(), returns status to a waiting parent, and has resources deallocated; parent-driven abort() and cascading termination cover other cases.
explanation: A terminated child whose table entry remains because its parent has not waited is a zombie. If the parent terminates without invoking wait(), the child is an orphan.

Cooperating processes exchange data through shared memory or message passing for information sharing, computation speedup, and modularity. Shared memory can avoid repeated kernel intervention after establishment, while message passing suits smaller data and distributed systems.

keyTerms.definition: A terminated process whose parent has not invoked wait().

commonMistakes.correction: It has terminated but retains a process-table entry until the parent waits.

examTips.body: Use kernel-intervention frequency to compare shared memory and message passing.

recap: exit returns status and releases resources.

materialSections.title: Shared memory and producer-consumer buffers
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Shared-memory communication is controlled by user processes after the region is established, so those processes must synchronize access and avoid simultaneous writes to one location.
explanation: An unbounded producer never waits, while a bounded producer waits on a full buffer; consumers wait on an empty buffer in either variation.

The circular bounded buffer uses in for the next free slot and out for the first full slot. With BUFFER_SIZE 10, the scheme holds at most nine items; in == out means empty, and ((in + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE) == out means full.

learningObjectives.text: Explain message-passing links, send/receive operations, and implementation choices.

materialSections.title: Message-passing operations and communication links
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Message passing lets processes communicate and synchronize without sharing an address space, which is especially useful across networked computers.
explanation: Processes use send(message) and receive(message) after a communication link is established. Link design considers participants, count, capacity, message size, and direction.

Logical link choices include direct or indirect naming, synchronous or asynchronous operations, and automatic or explicit buffering; physical implementations can use shared memory, a bus, or a network.

Processes use send(message) and receive(message) after a communication link is established. Link design considers participants, count, capacity, message size, and direction.

Logical link choices include direct or indirect naming, synchronous or asynchronous operations, and automatic or explicit buffering; physical implementations can use shared memory, a bus, or a network.

keyTerms.definition: IPC through exchanged messages without a shared address space.

workedExamples.body: Networked chat participants can communicate by message exchange.

examTips.body: Classify link issues as naming, synchronization, or buffering.

materialSections.title: Direct naming and mailbox-based communication
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Direct communication names the sender or recipient explicitly, whereas indirect communication routes messages through identified mailboxes or ports.
explanation: A direct link is automatic, connects exactly two processes, and is unique for that pair. Identifier changes can force updates to every reference.

A mailbox can connect two or more processes and support several links between a pair. The OS must support mailbox creation, sending, receiving, and deletion; mailbox ownership determines whether it disappears with a process. Shared receivers require a receiver-selection rule.

recap: Indirect communication requires a shared mailbox.

materialSections.title: Synchronization and buffering choices
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Blocking operations are synchronous, while non-blocking operations are asynchronous; blocking both send and receive creates a rendezvous.
explanation: Blocking send waits for receipt by a receiver or mailbox, and blocking receive waits for a message. A non-blocking receive returns either a valid message or null.

Temporary message queues may have zero, bounded, or unbounded capacity. Zero capacity forces sender-receiver rendezvous, bounded capacity blocks a sender only when full, and unbounded capacity never blocks a sender for space.

materialSections.title: Ordinary pipes, named pipes, and command pipelines
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: A pipe is an IPC channel whose design considers direction, duplex mode, process relationship, and whether communication crosses a network.
explanation: An ordinary pipe is unidirectional, normally requires a parent-child relationship, and uses a write end and a read end; two pipes are needed for two-way communication. Windows calls these anonymous pipes.
A named pipe is bidirectional, needs no parent-child relationship, and can serve several processes. In ls | less, ls produces directory output and less consumes it one screen at a time.

The example connects client 146.86.5.20:1625 to web server 161.25.19.8:80. Java supports connection-oriented TCP, connectionless UDP, and MulticastSocket for multiple recipients, followed by Date server and client examples.

materialSections.title: Multiprogramming and the CPU-I/O burst cycle
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Multiprogramming keeps a CPU core productive by running another process when the current one waits for I/O.
explanation: Process execution alternates CPU bursts and I/O bursts, begins with CPU work, and ends after a final CPU burst requests termination.
Measured workloads contain many short bursts and fewer long bursts. I/O-bound programs typically have many short CPU bursts, while CPU-bound programs have fewer long bursts.
materialSections.body:
Process execution alternates CPU bursts and I/O bursts, begins with CPU work, and ends after a final CPU burst requests termination.

Measured workloads contain many short bursts and fewer long bursts. I/O-bound programs typically have many short CPU bursts, while CPU-bound programs have fewer long bursts.

keyTerms.definition: An interval in which a process executes on the CPU.
An interval in which the process waits for I/O.

workedExamples.title: Multiprogramming
workedExamples.body: Another in-memory process takes the CPU when one process waits.

commonMistakes.misconception: CPU-bound programs usually have many short CPU bursts.
commonMistakes.correction: The lecture associates many short bursts with I/O-bound programs.

examTips.body: Use burst shape to distinguish I/O-bound from CPU-bound workloads.

recap: Only one process runs on a single core at once.

materialSections.title: Scheduler decisions, preemption, and dispatch
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: The CPU scheduler chooses a PCB from the ready queue, while the dispatcher transfers control to the selected process.
explanation: Scheduling can occur on running-to-waiting, running-to-ready, waiting-to-ready, or termination transitions. Restricting scheduling to the first and fourth makes it nonpreemptive; other choices enable preemption.

Preemption can expose inconsistent shared data if an update is interrupted. Dispatch performs a context switch, enters user mode, and jumps to the resume location; dispatch latency measures the stop-to-start interval.
materialSections.body:
Scheduling can occur on running-to-waiting, running-to-ready, waiting-to-ready, or termination transitions. Restricting scheduling to the first and fourth makes it nonpreemptive; other choices enable preemption.

Preemption can expose inconsistent shared data if an update is interrupted. Dispatch performs a context switch, enters user mode, and jumps to the resume location; dispatch latency measures the stop-to-start interval.

keyTerms.definition: Selects a ready process and allocates a CPU core.
Time for the dispatcher to stop one process and start another.

workedExamples.title: Race scenario
workedExamples.body: Preempting one process during a shared-data update can let another read inconsistent data.

commonMistakes.misconception: The scheduler and dispatcher perform the same role.
commonMistakes.correction: The scheduler selects; the dispatcher transfers CPU control.

examTips.body: List all three dispatcher actions in sequence.

recap: Ready queues can use several structures.
Nonpreemptive scheduling retains the CPU until release.
Dispatch speed matters at every switch.

materialSections.title: Scheduling criteria and algorithm families
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Scheduling algorithms are compared with CPU utilization, throughput, turnaround time, waiting time, and response time.
explanation: Utilization and throughput are maximized, while turnaround, waiting, and response times are minimized. Response time ends at the first response rather than completion.

Optimization often targets averages but may instead constrain an extreme, such as minimizing maximum response time. The lecture lists FCFS, SJF, RR, priority, multilevel queue, and multilevel feedback queue algorithms under a single-core assumption.

materialSections.title: SJF selection, example, and limitations
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: SJF chooses the ready process with the smallest next CPU burst and uses FCFS to break equal-burst ties.
explanation: SJF minimizes average waiting time for a fixed process set, but long jobs may starve when short jobs keep arriving and the next burst is not directly knowable.
The lecture example reports SJF waiting times 3, 16, 9, and 0, averaging 7 ms, compared with FCFS at 10.25 ms; the preceding FCFS example averages 8.75 ms for its stated workload.

materialSections.title: Predicting the next CPU burst
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: The next CPU burst can be predicted from measured history using an exponential average rather than known exactly.
explanation: The prediction combines the most recent burst tn with the previous prediction τn. Alpha weights recent versus past history: alpha zero ignores recent history, alpha one uses only the latest burst, and one-half weights them equally.

The initial τ0 may be constant or a system average. Expanding the recurrence shows that successive older terms receive decreasing weight when alpha and one minus alpha are at most one; the plotted example uses alpha one-half and τ0 of 10.

materialSections.title: Round-robin operation and examples
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Round robin adds timer-based preemption to FCFS and rotates unfinished processes to the tail of the ready queue after one time quantum.
explanation: A burst shorter than q releases the CPU voluntarily; a longer burst is interrupted and requeued. With n ready processes, each receives one-nth of CPU time in chunks no larger than q and waits no more than (n−1)q until its next quantum.

RR targets time sharing, response, fairness, and no starvation, but can have long waiting and higher turnaround than SJF. The q=4 example averages 5.66 ms waiting and 15.66 ms turnaround; the q=20 four-process example averages 73 ms waiting and 113.5 ms turnaround.

materialSections.title: Round-robin quantum, switches, and turnaround
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Round-robin performance depends strongly on q: a very large quantum approaches FCFS, while an extremely small quantum raises context-switch overhead.
explanation: A single 10-unit process makes zero switches with q=12, one with q=6, and nine with q=1. Three 10-unit processes average turnaround 20 with q=10 but 29 with q=1 before added switch cost.
The q=4 arrival-time example reports average waiting 11.75. A practical rule states that 80 percent of CPU bursts should be shorter than q, while q remains large relative to context-switch time.

materialSections.title: Priority scheduling and numerical examples

materialSections.summary: Priority scheduling selects the highest-priority process; under the lecture convention, the smallest integer is highest, and equal priorities use FCFS.

Scheduling occurs at two levels: the OS chooses a software thread for each logical CPU, then the physical core chooses which hardware thread executes, possibly by round robin.

materialSections.title: Load balancing, processor affinity, and NUMA
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Private SMP queues require load balancing so idle processors do not coexist with overloaded ones; a common ready queue does not require separate balancing.
explanation: Push migration uses a periodic task to move work away from overloaded processors, while pull migration lets an idle processor take work from a busy one.

Migration can discard warm-cache benefits. Soft affinity attempts to retain a processor without a guarantee; hard affinity limits execution to a specified processor set. A NUMA-aware OS places memory near the thread's CPU for faster access.
